c.tagline: Medieval towers, porticoes, and legendary cuisine.

emergency.note: 112 is the general EU number with interpreter support; 113 reaches the state police directly and 118 the ambulance service.

hood_landmark.Quadrilatero: medieval market lanes packed with food stalls and historic delis
hood_landmark.Santo Stefano: Basilica di Santo Stefano, the 'Seven Churches' complex
hood_landmark.Bolognina: the Mercato Albani covered market and the quarter's street art
hood_landmark.Saragozza: Portico di San Luca, the 666-arch climb to the Sanctuary of San Luca

avoid.reason: Pickpockets target the train station, Via dell'Indipendenza and crowded porticoes, and the Piazza Verdi university zone gets rowdy with drug dealing late at night.

hood_desc: Quadrilatero is the medieval market grid right behind Piazza Maggiore, packed with delis, wine bars and food stalls; ideal for first-time visitors and food lovers who want to be in the buzzing historic heart, though it gets crowded and touristy.

Santo Stefano centers on the beautiful basilica complex and its piazza, an elegant, atmospheric quarter of porticoed streets and aperitivo spots; suits those wanting classic Bologna charm and a refined but lively evening scene.

Bolognina is a gritty, multicultural former working-class district north of the station, now gentrifying with cheaper rents, ethnic eateries and a creative edge; good for budget travelers and those who prefer real local life over polish.

Saragozza is a quieter, residential and well-off zone leading up to the famous portico walk to San Luca; suits families and travelers who want calm, greenery and an authentic neighborhood feel within reach of the center.

San Donato is a large residential and university district east of the center with student energy, parkland and affordable housing; best for longer stays, students and visitors happy to trade central location for value and everyday local vibe.

water.note: Tap water meets EU standards and is safe to drink, though locals often prefer bottled for taste.

transit.pay: A single Tper ticket costs EUR 2.30 (about USD 2.70), valid 75 minutes; buy it at tabaccherie, newsstands and machines, or pay EUR 2.50 in coins at the onboard machine. Easiest option: tap a contactless bank card or phone on the validator when boarding (EUR 2.30, best fare applied automatically), or use the Roger app; a day ticket is EUR 9. The Marconi Express monorail to the airport is separate, EUR 12.80 one way (about USD 15), payable online, at station machines or by contactless tap at the gates.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5:30am to midnight; a network of dedicated night lines covers late-night hours, especially on weekends.

food.name: Tagliatelle al ragu
food.desc: Egg pasta cut eight millimetres wide, dressed in a slow meat ragu of beef, pancetta, soffritto and milk. Never spaghetti, never bolognese sauce.

places.name: Trattoria di Via Serra
places.note: Widely called the best ragu in the city; book roughly a month ahead.

places.name: Trattoria Anna Maria
places.note: Family-run for decades, pasta rolled fresh every morning by hand.

places.name: Osteria dell Orsa
places.note: No bookings, cheap plates, long queues; arrive before 7pm on weekdays.

food.name: Tortellini in brodo
food.desc: Thumbnail parcels of pork loin, prosciutto, mortadella and parmesan, floated in clear capon broth. Bologna most protected recipe.

places.name: Trattoria Anna Maria
places.note: Named by local guides as one of the best tortellini in brodo in Bologna.

places.name: Drogheria della Rosa
places.note: Old pharmacy turned trattoria, another of the city reference addresses.

places.name: Ristorante Grassilli
places.note: Long-established formal trattoria near Piazza Maggiore, strong on brodo.

food.name: Lasagne alla bolognese
food.desc: Green spinach pasta layered with ragu, bechamel and parmesan, baked until the top corners go crisp. Denser and less tomato-heavy than exports.

places.name: Trattoria Da Me
places.note: Makes all its pasta in a lab metres from the dining room; book ahead.

places.name: Trattoria di Via Serra
places.note: Obsessive sourcing from small Apennine producers shows in the baked pasta.

places.name: Osteria dell Orsa
places.note: Student-priced version of the classics, served all day without fuss.

food.name: Mortadella di Bologna
food.desc: Silky pink pork sausage studded with fat cubes, pistachios and black pepper. Sliced paper thin and eaten warm with gnocco fritto.

places.name: Salumeria Simoni
places.note: Historic deli in the old market lanes with a tasting room upstairs.

places.name: Tamburini
places.note: Century-old salumeria and self-service counter in the heart of the food quarter.

places.name: Mercato di Mezzo
places.note: Covered market hall with salumi counters and standing tables for a quick plate.

food.name: Crescentine e gnocco fritto
food.desc: Puffed pillows of fried dough and small griddled breads, served hot to wrap round mortadella, squacquerone cheese and prosciutto.

places.name: Tamburini
places.note: Classic aperitivo plate of fried dough and cured meats in the old market.

places.name: Trattoria Da Me
places.note: Modern trattoria that still opens the meal with the traditional fried breads.

places.name: Mercato di Mezzo
places.note: Several counters serve gnocco fritto with Emilian salumi and a glass of Pignoletto.

food.name: Cotoletta alla petroniana
food.desc: Breaded veal cutlet topped with prosciutto and parmesan, then finished in broth until the cheese melts. Bologna richest main course.

places.name: Ristorante Diana
places.note: Historic dining room that has kept the old Bolognese main courses on the menu.

places.name: Trattoria Anna Maria
places.note: Technically precise traditional kitchen covering the full local repertoire.

places.name: Ristorante Grassilli
places.note: Old-guard trattoria doing the classic veal and broth preparations.

food.name: Lambrusco
food.desc: Dry fizzy red from Emilia, served cold and purple-frothed. Its acidity is built to cut through ragu, mortadella and fried dough.

places.name: Osteria del Sole
places.note: Wine-only tavern since 1465; buy food elsewhere and carry it in.

places.name: Enoteca Italiana
places.note: Long-running wine bar and shop with a deep Emilian by-the-glass list.

places.name: Mercato di Mezzo
places.note: Market bars pour Lambrusco alongside plates of salumi all afternoon.

food.name: Pignoletto dei Colli Bolognesi
food.desc: Crisp, faintly bitter white from the hills just south of the city, often lightly sparkling. The local aperitivo before anyone says spritz.

places.name: Enoteca Italiana
places.note: Good selection of Colli Bolognesi growers, tasted at the counter.

places.name: Osteria del Sole
places.note: Bologna oldest drinking room, cheap glasses and communal tables.

places.name: Tamburini
places.note: Pairs local whites with its salumi and fried-dough plates at aperitivo hour.

landmarks: Two Towers (Le Due Torri)
Bologna's leaning medieval Asinelli and Garisenda towers are the city's defining silhouette and most photographed symbol.
Piazza Maggiore
The grand central square lined with medieval palaces, forming the heart of Bologna's historic center and a classic wide shot.
Basilica di San Petronio
A massive Gothic basilica with an unfinished pink-and-white marble facade dominating Piazza Maggiore.
Fountain of Neptune (Fontana del Nettuno)
A celebrated Renaissance bronze fountain by Giambologna, an elegant focal point just off Piazza Maggiore.
Portico di San Luca
The world's longest portico, a nearly 4-km covered arcaded walkway climbing scenically to a hilltop sanctuary.
Bologna Cathedral (Metropolitan Cathedral of San Pietro)
The city's baroque-fronted cathedral, notable for its bell tower and richly decorated interior.
Archiginnasio of Bologna
A 16th-century former university building famed for its frescoed courtyard and historic anatomical theatre.
Basilica di Santo Stefano (Seven Churches)
A unique complex of interconnected medieval churches and cloisters, prized for its atmospheric brick architecture.
Palazzo d'Accursio (Palazzo Comunale)
Bologna's historic town hall with a striking clock tower and courtyard, anchoring Piazza Maggiore's skyline.
Finestrella di Via Piella
A tiny window revealing a hidden canal view nicknamed 'Little Venice,' one of Bologna's most charming photo surprises.

train.note: All trains leave from Bologna Centrale. Daytime EuroCity/Railjet runs north via Verona and the Brenner Pass to Munich; the ÖBB Nightjet sleeper links Bologna with Munich, Salzburg and Vienna overnight. Travel is within Schengen, so no passport check on board.

bus.note: International coaches use Bologna Autostazione, just north of the centre. FlixBus is the main long-distance operator; Italian domestic coaches (Itabus, Flixbus) also start here.

ferry.note: Bologna is inland with no ferry service. The nearest ports for Adriatic ferries to Croatia and Greece are Ancona and Ravenna (both reachable by train in 1-2 hours).
